title: Directive Principles

cards.h: A promise that courts cannot enforce, yet cannot ignore
cards.b:
The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in Part IV (Articles 36-51) set the goals of a welfare state: a fair share of resources, decent work, education, health, and peace. They are non-justiciable: no one can go to court to compel the State to follow them (Article 37).

Yet Article 37 also says they are "fundamental in the governance of the country" and that the State must apply them when making laws. This tension is what examiners test.

Typical questions: Are the DPSP useful or only "pious wishes"? What is the relation between Part III and Part IV? How have courts used the DPSP? Which amendments gave the DPSP priority?

The idea comes from the Irish Constitution (1937), and, in spirit, from the welfare ideals of the freedom movement, including the Karachi Resolution (1931) on fundamental rights and economic policy.
Part IV was drafted with the advice of B.N. Rau. Later amendments added Articles 39A, 43A, 48A (42nd, 1976), 43B (97th, 2011) and changed 45 (86th, 2002).

cards.h: Granville Austin and Ambedkar on the DPSP
cards.b:
Granville Austin, Cornerstone of a Nation (1966)

Part III and Part IV together are "the conscience of the Constitution". They form a seamless web: rights give political freedom; directives aim at social and economic justice. Austin saw them as the heart of the "social revolution".

B.R. Ambedkar, Constituent Assembly, November 1948

The directives are "instruments of instructions" to those who govern. A government that ignores them may face voters at the next election. He wanted economic democracy, not only political democracy. Ambedkar warned that political equality without social and economic equality would be a contradiction (speech of 25 November 1949).

K.T. Shah's critique

Shah is widely credited with calling them a cheque on a bank payable at the bank's convenience. The sharper point: a right without a remedy is weak.

Shriman Narayan Agarwal, Gandhian Constitution for Free India (1946)

The source for the Gandhian directives such as village panchayats and cottage industry.

cards.h: Part III versus Part IV: the long legal contest
cards.b:
1. Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Directive Principles must "run subordinate" to rights. Parliament answered with the First Amendment (1951).
  2. Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights.
  3. 25th Amendment (1971): added Article 31C, protecting laws made to implement Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31.
  4. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): upheld Article 31C in part, but struck down the bar on judicial review.
  5. 42nd Amendment (1976): extended Article 31C to all Directive Principles.
  6. Minerva Mills (1980): struck down this extension. The Court said the Constitution rests on a balance between Parts III and IV, and giving absolute priority to either would destroy it.

Since 1980 courts read them together. The Directive Principles are used to give meaning to rights and to test whether restrictions on rights are reasonable.

cards.h: How the Court has used the Directive Principles
cards.b:
• Education: Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993) read a right to education into Article 21 through Article 41 and 45. The 86th Amendment (2002) then inserted Article 21A.
  • Equal pay: Randhir Singh (1982) used Article 39(d).
  • Bonded labour: Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984).
  • Livelihood: Olga Tellis (1985), from Article 39(a) and 41.
  • Legal aid: Article 39A shaped Hussainara Khatoon (1979), on prisoners awaiting trial.
  • Environment: Article 48A in the M.C. Mehta cases.
  • Cow slaughter: State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005) upheld bans, relying on Article 48.
  • Resources: in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (5 November 2024), a nine-judge bench held, by majority, that not every private resource is a "material resource of the community" under Article 39(b), limiting the sweeping view of earlier cases.

Many programmes put the directives into action:

  • Article 40: the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave local bodies a constitutional base.
  • Article 39 and 41: the zamindari abolition, land ceilings, MGNREGA (2005), and the National Food Security Act (2013), which covers about two-thirds of the population.
  • Article 43: minimum wages laws and the four labour codes (in force from 21 November 2025).
  • Article 45 and 21A: the Right to Education Act (2009) and early childhood care under the National Education Policy 2020.
  • Article 47: public health missions, and alcohol prohibition in some states (Gujarat, Bihar and Nagaland).
  • Article 44: the Uniform Civil Code remains incomplete. Goa has its old Portuguese-era code. Uttarakhand passed a UCC law in 2025. The 22nd Law Commission invited views on a UCC in June-July 2023.
  • Article 50: the judiciary was separated from the executive in most states by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

Link Part IV to ideas you studied in Paper I Section A.

  • Positive liberty and social rights. Rights in Part III are mostly negative: the State must not interfere. The directives ask the State to act: to feed, educate and employ. This follows T.H. Green and the later welfare-liberal tradition.
  • Rawls. Article 38(2) (reduce inequalities in income, status and opportunities) and Article 39(b)-(c) (resources not concentrated) echo the difference principle and the concern with the basic structure.
  • Marx and socialism. The "socialistic" group seeks a more equal economy without abolishing private property. Critics on the left call this too mild.
  • Gandhi. Village self-rule (Article 40), cottage industry (43) and prohibition (47) reflect Hind Swaraj and trusteeship ideas.

Three key differences from Part III:

Fundamental Rights: enforceable by courts; limit the State; mostly civil and political; individuals hold them.
Directive Principles: not enforceable; guide the State; mostly social and economic; the community benefits.

Case for them:

  • They shape policy and legislation and give courts a basis to read social justice into rights.
  • They help voters judge governments on performance.
  • Many have become rights through later laws (education, food, work).

Case against:

  • They are unenforceable, so governments pick and choose. For example, the UCC and prohibition have been pursued unevenly.
  • They are a mixed bag of ideas: some contradictory (a free market and a socialistic order) or outdated (prohibition).
  • Some are used to justify majoritarian policy (Article 48 cattle laws).
  • Fiscal limits and "freebies" debates: the Court has been asked to define welfare versus populist giveaways.

Balanced view: DPSP are the moral and political compass of the State, not a court-enforced list. Their strength is in democratic pressure and in judicial interpretation.

• UCC: Uttarakhand's 2025 law is the first by a state since Independence (Goa's civil code is a Portuguese-era law); a national UCC has not been enacted.
  • 39(b): the November 2024 ruling matters for land, redistribution and tax debates.
  • Article 41, 47: food security, cash transfers and women-targeted schemes.
  • Article 48A and 51A(g): climate rulings such as M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024).
  • Article 40: the state of panchayats' powers and finances.
  • Article 51: India's foreign policy values, such as peace and respect for international law, are cited in strategic autonomy debates.

"Directive Principles are the conscience of the Constitution. Do they have any legal force?"

Structure: define Part IV and Article 37; three groups with Articles; Austin and Ambedkar; the legal contest (Champakam to Minerva Mills); key judgments and laws that gave them life; critique; recent issues (39(b) 2024, UCC); balanced conclusion.
